paras: The lynching of James Spencer was the killing of a Black railway postal clerk by masked men near Basic City, Mississippi, in the summer of 1920, while an officer was taking him to answer a charge of assaulting a white fellow clerk. Lauderdale County's new circuit judge, C. C. Miller, singled out the case in his charge to the grand jury in August, but the grand jury reported that it could not find evidence to indict anyone for the county's mob violence.

Spencer, described as a "negro" railway postal clerk, was charged with assaulting Otho Parker, a white postal clerk, while the two worked in the mail car of a train passing through Clarke County. The Age-Herald's dispatch called the charge "assault with intent," while the News Scimitar described it as assault with a knife and placed the fight in the mail car. The date of the alleged assault and of the killing is not given in the coverage, beyond that the lynching came after the county's February court term and was called "recent" on August 2.

Spencer was being taken to Enterprise, in Clarke County, "in charge of an officer" when masked men stopped them near Basic City and shot him to death. The Age-Herald described the killers as "a small party of masked men" and gave no number. Nothing in the coverage says what the officer did or whether anyone else was present.

On August 2 Judge Miller, sitting for the first time after his appointment by Governor Russell, opened the criminal term in Meridian and charged the grand jury specially on the lynching. He also called attention to recent attempts by mobs to force the county jail to seize two other prisoners, Percy Thompson and Ludie Martin, and asked the jurors to bring the guilty parties to justice. After eight days the grand jury, with W. T. Rainey as foreman, returned 33 true bills and expressed its "disapproval of mob violence," but reported that it was "unable to obtain evidence sufficient to find indictments" against the mobs. The report did not name Spencer, and no arrest or indictment in his killing was found in the coverage.

The killing itself does not appear in the August coverage; the case reached print as one item in reports on the Lauderdale County court term. A Meridian preview printed in the Birmingham Age-Herald on August 2 and in the Brookhaven Semi-Weekly Leader on August 4 listed it among the term's cases as a lynching "following his attack" on Parker, stating the accusation as fact. The Age-Herald's report of the judge's charge ran under the headline "GRAND JURY TOLD TO GO AFTER MOB," and the Memphis News Scimitar gave the only account of where and how Spencer died in a single sentence of a story headed "BUSY SESSION AHEAD FOR COURT AT MERIDIAN."

The Chicago Whip carried the story on its front page on August 14 under the headline "DEMANDS LYNCHERS INDICTMENT." Its text followed the Age-Herald's account of the judge's charge but spoke of "the lynchers who murdered James Spencer, a colored postal clerk," and changed the judge's reference to disregard of the law "by mobs" to disregard "by certain white men of the state of Mississippi." No Black-press account of the killing itself or of the grand jury's outcome was found.

reader.title: Lynching of James Spencer
bases: Masked men shot to death a Black prisoner charged with assaulting a white fellow clerk while an officer was taking him to court, and the judge, the grand jury notices and the Black press all called it a lynching (A2, A4, A6).

Spencer was shot to death by masked men who took him while he was in an officer's charge to answer an assault charge, which every report calls a lynching (A2, A4, A6); the size of the 'small party of masked men' is not given, so a group of three or more is likely but not stated (A2).

Separate Meridian dispatches in the Age-Herald and the News Scimitar, and the Chicago Whip, agree that James Spencer, a Black postal clerk, was lynched by masked men while charged with assaulting a white clerk (A2, A4, A6), though all are reports of the grand jury term, not first reports of the killing.

accounts.label: Meridian court correspondents
accounts.gist: Spencer, a Black postal clerk charged with assaulting white clerk Otho Parker in the mail car, was shot to death by masked men near Basic City while an officer was taking him to Clarke County; the new circuit judge charged the grand jury to investigate.

accounts.label: Grand jury final report
accounts.gist: The grand jury disapproved of mob violence in the county and said it could not obtain evidence sufficient to indict anyone for 'these mobs'.

accounts.label: Black press (Chicago Whip)
accounts.gist: The judge demanded that the grand jury indict 'the lynchers who murdered James Spencer'; the Whip attributed the lawlessness to 'certain white men of the state of Mississippi'.

framing.detail: The Meridian preview listed the lynching among the term's 'sensational' cases as following 'his attack on Otto Parker', stating the accusation as fact.
The Age-Herald headlined 'GRAND JURY TOLD TO GO AFTER MOB' and reported the judge's condemnation of the 'reckless disregard of the law by mobs'.
The News Scimitar gave the only account of place and manner in one sentence of a 'busy session' court story.
The Chicago Whip ran it on page one as 'DEMANDS LYNCHERS INDICTMENT', calling the killers 'the lynchers who murdered' Spencer and naming 'certain white men' as lawbreakers.

conflicts.note: The versions are compatible; only the Aug. 1 preview states the alleged attack as fact rather than as a charge.
